Pairing symmetry and superconductivity from long-range Coulomb interactions in the extended tt-t′t^{\prime}-t′′t^{\prime\prime}-JzJ_{z} model for cuprates

U. A. Diaz-Reynoso Correspondence email address: udiazr@ens.cnyn.unam.mx Affiliation: Departamento de Física, Centro de Nanociencias y Nanotecnología, Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, Apartado Postal 14, 22800, Ensenada, Baja California, México    F. Mireles  Correspondence email address: fmireles@ens.cnyn.unam.mx Affiliation: Departamento de Física, Centro de Nanociencias y Nanotecnología, Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, Apartado Postal 14, 22800, Ensenada, Baja California, México
September 16, 2026
Abstract

We investigate the pairing symmetry of the ground-state phase diagram of an extended two-dimensional tt-t′t^{\prime}-t′′t^{\prime\prime}-JzJ_{z} model, in which the first-, second-, and third-nearest neighbor electron hopping terms (t,t′t,t^{\prime} and t′′t^{\prime\prime}) and an anisotropic Ising-like antiferromagnetic interaction JzJ_{z} are treated on the same framework. We find that the dominant pairing symmetry depends sensitively on the sign and magnitude of the hopping parameters t′t^{\prime} and t′′t^{\prime\prime}, showing pure pp-wave, pure dd-wave, or coexisting pairing channels, highlighting the decisive role of these terms. We further explore the role of the long-range and short-range repulsive interactions in the formation of pairs and analyze the specific case of hole-doped cuprates. Our results indicate that repulsive interactions favors hole pair escaping of the stripe domains. Furthermore, pairing correlation calculations strongly suggest that repulsive Coulomb interactions drive reentrant superconducting behavior at experimentally observed underdoped regime (δ≈0.07\delta\approx 0.07 to 0.150.15), as in Neodymium-based cuprates.

I Introduction

Strongly correlated materials, such as high-TcT_{c} superconducting cuprates remain of current interest as their phase diagram is still not fully understood[1, 2]. The phase diagram feature intertwined antiferromagnetic, pseudogap, strange metal, and superconducting phases, whose interplay continues to be the subject of active debate. [3, 4, 5, 7, 6]. Simplified theoretical models such as the Hubbard and tt-JJ models have succeeded in describing several aspects of quasi-two-dimensional cuprates, as competing inhomogeneous orders in the underdoped regime, including superconductivity [10, 11, 8, 9] and the appearance of unidirectional stripe ordering [12] – corresponding to a self-induced antiphase domain walls of antiferromgnetic spins [13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19]. Nevertheless, most models fail to reproduce superconductivity over a wide doping range for hole-doped cuprates, particularly the the well known anomaly near the hole doping of δ≈1/8\delta\approx 1/8. Although some variants that include longer-range hoppings, such as t′t^{\prime} and t′′t^{\prime\prime}, successfully capture pairing on the electron-doped side [9, 8], the hole-doped regime systematically yields non-superconducting stripe ground states, suggesting that additional physical ingredients are essential [16, 20].

Experimental reports on Nd-doped La2-xSrxCuO4 (Nd-LSCO) indicate superconducting behavior across a wide range 0.055<δ<0.200.055<\delta<0.20, with a notable suppression at δ≈0.12\delta\approx 0.12. This suppression is accompanied by the stabilization of static charge and spin stripe order, as observed via neutron scattering and muon spin rotation experiments [21, 13, 22]. At this critical doping, parallel-ordered stripes  [23] emerge, suggesting their competition and coexistence with the superconducting phase  [24, 25, 26]. This puzzling behavior poses a substantial challenge to theoretical models and numerical studies of high-TcT_{c} superconductivity.

A common approach to include electron correlations in simplified lattice models is through the inclusion of an on-site Hubbard repulsion UU. However, ab initio calculations  [28, 27] and experimental [29, 30] results points that the nearest-neighbor repulsion VV can be also significant in LSCO compounds, with typical ratios |V/U|≈0.15|V/U|\approx 0.15–0.60.6. Including only short-range repulsive interactions has proven insufficient; at the estimated values of VV, superconductivity is usually suppressed[31]. Earlier studies of long-range repulsive interactions were performed with the aim of avoiding phase separation  [32, 33, 34]. Nevertheless, phase separation can be avoided without such long-range terms; stripe phases were observed as the ground state in powerful density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) calculations on long cylinders  [35, 36]. The stripe ordering found in these calculations were half-filled, consistent with the experiments of Tranquada et al. [13]. This agreement strengthen confidence in the model and subsequently triggered the neglect of long-range repulsive interactions.

However, there is an issue with these striped solutions: they do not exhibit superconductivity in the expected range δ≤1/8\delta\leq 1/8 [16]. The inclusion of second- and third-neighbor hopping amplitudes (t′t^{\prime} and t′′t^{\prime\prime}) has allowed indeed a more comprehensive description of a wide range of phenomena in cuprates. For instance Jiang et al.  [9, 8, 20] mapped the ground- state phase diagram over a broad parameter space of t′t^{\prime} and t′′t^{\prime\prime}. For electron-doped cuprates, they found dx2−y2d_{x^{2}-y^{2}} superconductivity. For hole-doped cuprates, however, they observed only non-superconducting stripes, indicating that a key ingredient is still missing.

The aim of this work is precisely to tackle this issue. To that end, we first perform a systematic investigation of the pairing symmetry in the ground-state phase diagram of the two-dimensional tt-t′t^{\prime}-t′′t^{\prime\prime}-JzJ_{z} model, combining symmetry-based analysis with numerical calculations. We then extend the model by incorporating long-range repulsive interactions, and explore the mechanism by which superconducting pairs escape the non-superconducting stripes across a broad doping range, thus restoring the superconducting phase.

II Model Hamiltonian

The minimal lattice Hamiltonian employed in this work is derived from the large-UU limit of the Hubbard model (|U/t|≫1|U/t|\gg 1), in which double occupancy is forbidden. The Hamiltonian comprises three additive terms: (i) a kinetic part accounting for first-, second-, and third-nearest neighbor hopping, Ht​-​t′​-​t′′H_{t\text{-}t^{\prime}\text{-}t^{\prime\prime}}, (ii) a near neighbor Ising-type magnetic exchange term HJzH_{J_{z}}, and (iii) a long-range Coulomb repulsive interaction, HVH_{V}. It reads

H=Ht​-​t′​-​t′′+HJz+HV.\displaystyle H=H_{t\text{-}t^{\prime}\text{-}t^{\prime\prime}}+H_{J_{z}}+H_{V}. (1)

The first two terms of the right conform the known t​-​t′​-​t′′​-​Jz{t\text{-}t^{\prime}\text{-}t^{\prime\prime}\text{-}J_{z}} model.

(i) Kinetic contribution: the kinetic part of the Hamiltonian (1) is given by

Ht−t′−t′′\displaystyle H_{t-t^{\prime}-t^{\prime\prime}} =(−t∑⟨𝒊,𝒋⟩​σ−t′∑⟨⟨𝒊,𝒋⟩⟩​σ−t′′∑⟨⟨⟨𝒊,𝒋⟩⟩⟩​σ)c𝒊​σ†c𝒋​σ+h.c.\displaystyle=\Bigg(-t\!\!\sum_{\langle\bm{i,j}\rangle\sigma}-t^{\prime}\!\!\!\!\sum_{\langle\langle\bm{i},\bm{j}\rangle\rangle\sigma}-t^{\prime\prime}\!\!\!\!\!\!\sum_{\langle\langle\langle\bm{i},\bm{j}\rangle\rangle\rangle\sigma}\Bigg)c_{\bm{i}\sigma}^{\dagger}c_{\bm{j}\sigma}+\text{h.c.} (2)

Here, c𝒊​σ†c_{\bm{i}\sigma}^{\dagger} and c𝒊​σc_{\bm{i}\sigma} are the creation and annihilation electron operators with spin σ={↑,↓}\sigma=\{\uparrow,\downarrow\} at the vector position 𝒊=(x,y){\bm{i}}=(x,y) being xx and yy the particle coordinates in lattice units. The sums over ⟨𝒊,𝒋⟩\langle\bm{i},\bm{j}\rangle, ⟨⟨𝒊,𝒋⟩⟩\langle\langle\bm{i},\bm{j}\rangle\rangle, and ⟨⟨⟨𝒊,𝒋⟩⟩⟩\langle\langle\langle\bm{i},\bm{j}\rangle\rangle\rangle run over first, second, and third nearest neighbors bonds, with corresponding hopping amplitudes t,t′t,t^{\prime} and t′′t^{\prime\prime}, respectively.

The sign of t′t^{\prime} is related to the doping type: t′>0t^{\prime}>0 for electron-doped and t′<0t^{\prime}<0 for hole-doped cuprates. Thus, t′t^{\prime} is essential for capturing the electron-hole asymmetry. Notably, the estimated values in cuprates, |t′/t|≈0.3|t^{\prime}/t|\approx 0.3 and |t′′/t|≈0.2|t^{\prime\prime}/t|\approx 0.2 [28, 37], render these terms non-negligible. Although several studies have examined pairing symmetries in related models  [38, 39], our analysis reveals how the sign and magnitude of t′t^{\prime} and t′′t^{\prime\prime} govern both the existence and the symmetry of pairs. Additionally, we demonstrate that certain symmetries forbid specific states, thereby modifying the pair characteristics.

One might also consider the three-site hopping term. Nevertheless, Leung et al. [37] showed that, although it provides minor refinements, it is not essential for reproducing Angle-Resolved Photoemission Spectroscopy (ARPES) data within the tt-t′t^{\prime}-t′′t^{\prime\prime}-JzJ_{z} model. Given that this term acts on second- and third-neighbor sites, we believe its effects are effectively masked by t′t^{\prime} and t′′t^{\prime\prime} terms. For simplicity, we therefore omit it in the present work.

(ii) Spin exchange interaction: Within the large-UU limit, the Hubbard model reduces via canonical transformation to the tt-JJ model, with superexchange J=4​t2/|U|J=4t^{2}/|U|. To reduce computational cost, we further adopt the Ising approximation (Jz​S𝒊z​S𝒋zJ_{z}S_{\bm{i}}^{z}S_{\bm{j}}^{z}) instead of the full vector exchange (J​𝐒𝒊⋅𝐒𝒋J\mathbf{S}_{\bm{i}}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{\bm{j}} ), yielding to an Ising-like magnetic interaction. The nearest neighbor spin exchange Hamiltonian is thus

HJz=J​∑⟨𝒊,𝒋⟩(S𝒊z​S𝒋z−n𝒊​n𝒋4),\displaystyle H_{J_{z}}=J\sum_{\langle\bm{i},\bm{j}\rangle}\left(S_{\bm{i}}^{z}S_{\bm{j}}^{z}-\frac{n_{\bm{i}}n_{\bm{j}}}{4}\right), (3)

where the occupation operator n𝒊=n𝒊↑+n𝒊↓n_{\bm{i}}=n_{\bm{i}\uparrow}+n_{\bm{i}\downarrow}, n𝒊​σ=c𝒊​σ†​c𝒊​σn_{\bm{i}\sigma}=c_{\bm{i}\sigma}^{\dagger}c_{\bm{i}\sigma}, and S𝒊z=12​(n𝒊↑−n𝒊↓)S_{\bm{i}}^{z}=\frac{1}{2}(n_{\bm{i}\uparrow}-n_{\bm{i}\downarrow}) is the zz-component of the quantum spin operator 𝐒𝒊\mathbf{S}_{\bm{i}}. The tt-JzJ_{z} model retains most of the key physical phenomena of the tt-JJ model, particularly pairing and stripe correlations [40, 41]. In some cases, both models yield qualitatively and quantitatively similar results upon scaling JJ by a factor [42]. Typical values of JJ for cuprates are around J∼0.3J\sim 0.3–0.50.5 [43, 8]. We set J=0.4J=0.4 in this work.

(iii) Repulsive long-range interactions: Screening effects in metals and complex oxides are commonly modeled through Yukawa-type potentials, V(r)∝e−r/λ/rV(r)\propto e^{-r/\lambda}/r, where λ\lambda denotes the screening length. However, this result is rooted in the Thomas–Fermi approximation, whose underlying assumptions are free-particle behavior and three-dimensional isotropy. In contrast, La2-xSrxCuO4 (LSCO) is a prototypical two-dimensional bad metal, characterized by an in-plane resistivity approximately 500 times that of copper, a highly anisotropic orthorhombic structure (c/a=2.44c/a=2.44), and an out-of-plane to in-plane resistivity ratio ρc/ρa​b>103\rho_{c}/\rho_{ab}>10^{3}  [44]. Consequently, the weak interlayer coupling and large interplane spacing act to significantly suppress screening. Moreover, recent studies show that long-range interactions persist even in two-dimensional metallic systems [45], and a theoretical analysis of stripes under repulsive interactions concluded that long-range stripe order can arise from a generalized dipolar interaction 1/rα1/r^{\alpha} only for α<2\alpha<2 [46]. These observations motivate us to adopt a long-range Coulomb repulsive potential of the form,

HV=∑𝒊≠𝒋V2​|𝒊−𝒋|​n𝒊​n𝒋.\displaystyle H_{V}=\sum_{\bm{i}\neq\bm{j}}\frac{V}{2|{\bm{i}}-{\bm{j}}|}n_{\bm{i}}n_{\bm{j}}. (4)

The distance |𝒓|=|𝒊−𝒋||\bm{r}|=|{\bm{i}}-{\bm{j}}| (in lattice units) used in this work is that of the Clifford torus [47]. The Clifford torus is a two-dimensional flat manifold that can be regarded as the product of two circles embedded in a four-dimensional space. The induced metric is a smooth function of its coordinates. This coordinate mapping has been used previously in tt-JJ models with long-range interactions [48, 49] and to efficiently calculate the energy of periodic and infinite charge distributions as well as the Madelung constant [50, 51]. The distance on the Clifford torus is given explicitly by

|𝒓|=|(x,y)|=x′2+y′2,\displaystyle|\bm{r}|=|(x,y)|=\sqrt{x^{\prime 2}+y^{\prime 2}}, (5)

with x′,y′x^{\prime},y^{\prime} defined as

x′​(x)\displaystyle x^{\prime}(x) =Lπ​sin⁡(π​|x|/L),\displaystyle=\frac{L}{\pi}\sin(\pi|x| / L), (6)
y′​(y)\displaystyle y^{\prime}(y) =Mπ​sin⁡(π​|y|/M),\displaystyle=\frac{M}{\pi}\sin(\pi|y| / M), (7)

where LL and MM are the length and width of the system (per lattice width). Hence N=L×MN=L\times M as the total number of lattice sites. The value of VV can be inferred from ab initio calculations [28]. From the difference between first- and second-nearest neighbor potentials, V1−V2=1.44V_{1}-V_{\sqrt{2}}=1.44 (in units of |t||t|), we obtain V≈4.9V\approx 4.9, while from the first- and third-neighbor potentials, V1−V2=2.65V_{1}-V_{2}=2.65, we get V≈5.3V\approx 5.3.

III Numerical Method

The ground-state properties of the extended Hamiltonian (1) are obtained via a truncated Lanczos method[53, 54]. This approach combines a variational principle with iterative Hilbert-space reduction and exact diagonalization through the standard Lanczos algorithm applied in successive subspaces. The geometry of the system consist of a rectangular lattice comprising N=L×MN=L\times M sites, subject to fully periodic boundary conditions. The procedure starts from a trial state |Ψ𝒌⟩\ket{\Psi_{\bm k}} in an nn-dimensional Hilbert space and iteratively constructs eigenstates from a local basis of the form

|Ψ𝒌⟩=∑𝑹a𝑹​|𝒌;𝑹⟩=∑𝑹a𝑹​P^𝒌N𝒌,𝑹​|𝑹⟩,\displaystyle\ket{\Psi_{\bm k}}=\sum_{\bm{R}}a_{\bm{R}}\ket{\bm k;\bm R}=\sum_{\bm{R}}a_{\bm{R}}\frac{\hat{P}_{\bm{k}}}{\sqrt{N_{\bm{k},\bm{R}}}}\ket{\bm R}, (8)

where a𝑹∈ℂa_{\bm{R}}\in\mathbb{C}, and |𝑹⟩=c†𝒊1,σ1c†𝒊2,σ2⋯|0⟩\ket{\bm R}=c^{\dagger}_{\bm{i}_{1},\sigma_{1}}c^{\dagger}_{\bm{i}_{2},\sigma_{2}}\cdots\ket{0} describes a configuration state, where c𝒊ν,σν†c^{\dagger}_{\bm{i}_{\nu},\sigma_{\nu}} is the creation operator of a Wannier state of a ν\nu-th electron at the vector position 𝒊ν\bm{i}_{\nu} with spin σν={↑,↓}\sigma_{\nu}=\{\uparrow,\downarrow\}. Here, P^𝒌\hat{P}_{\bm{k}} denotes the projector operator defined by

P^𝒌=1N​∑𝒓ei​𝒌⋅𝒓​T^𝒓,\displaystyle\hat{P}_{\bm{k}}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\bm{r}}e^{i\bm{k}\cdot\bm{r}}\hat{T}_{\bm{r}}, (9)

such that N𝒌,𝑹=⟨𝑹|​P^𝒌​|𝑹⟩≠0N_{\bm{k},\bm{R}}=\bra{\bm R}\hat{P}_{\bm{k}}\ket{\bm R}\neq 0, and the operator T^𝒓\hat{T}_{\bm{r}} translates a creation or annihilation operator from position 𝒊\bm{i} to 𝒊+𝒓\bm{i}+\bm{r},

T^𝒓​c𝒊†​T^𝒓†=c𝒊+𝒓†.\displaystyle\hat{T}_{\bm{r}}c^{\dagger}_{\bm{i}}\hat{T}^{\dagger}_{\bm{r}}=c^{\dagger}_{\bm{i}+\bm{r}}. (10)

At each iteration, the Hilbert space is enlarged by acting the Hamiltonian HH to the current state |Ψ𝒌⟩\ket{\Psi_{\bm k}}; which is diagonalized within this expanded subspace, and then the space is truncated to retain only the γ​n\gamma n states with the largest amplitudes (γ>1\gamma>1). This cycle is repeated until convergence. When combined with a block Lanczos extension, the method is used to obtain the energy of a few low lying states. The trial wavefunction is typically initialized as a single configuration |𝑹⟩\ket{\bm R}—for example, the Néel state with a few holes, or suitable configuration states candidates to the ground state.

We found that for the systems analyzed, states with zero total momentum (𝒌=0\bm{k}=0), have the lowest energy. All systems analyzed have total spin zz-component Stotalz=0S^{z}_{\text{total}}=0 (equal number of ↑\uparrow and ↓\downarrow electrons). The total energy of a state |Ψ0⟩\ket{\Psi_0} is given by E=⟨Ψ0|​H​|Ψ0⟩E=\bra{\Psi_0}H\ket{\Psi_0}. The magnetic energy is EJz=⟨Ψ0|​HJz​|Ψ0⟩E_{J_{z}}=\bra{\Psi_0}H_{J_{z}}\ket{\Psi_0} and the Coulomb energy is EV=⟨Ψ0|​HV​|Ψ0⟩E_{V}=\bra{\Psi_0}H_{V}\ket{\Psi_0}. At V=0V=0 and no holes, the ground state within this model for a lattice of size L×ML\times M with both L,ML,M even is the Néel state with energy E0=−L​M​JE_{0}=-LMJ. For a lattice with LL odd and MM even, the ground state is similar to a Néel state but features a defect domain wall of length MM, giving E0=−L​M​J+M​J/2E_{0}=-LMJ+MJ/2. The standard practice is to measure the energy per hole rather than the total energy. The energy per hole is thus defined as

ℰ={(E−E0)/nhfor L,M even(E−E0+M​J/2)/nhfor L odd, M even\displaystyle{\cal E}=\begin{cases}\left(E-E_{0}\right)/n_{h}\quad&\text{for $L,M$ even}\\ \left(E-E_{0}+MJ/2\right)/n_{h}\quad&\text{for $L$ odd, $M$ even}\end{cases} (11)

where nhn_{h} is the number of holes and E0E_{0} is the ground state energy without holes. We define the electric charge energy per hole as ℰV=EV/nh{\cal E}_{V}=E_{V}/n_{h} and the tt-JzJ_{z} energy per hole as ℰt−Jz=ℰ−ℰV{\cal E}_{t-J_{z}}={\cal E}-{\cal E}_{V}, which gives the energy (per hole) of the system in the absence of Coulomb electron repulsion.

IV Results and discussion

We begin by analyzing the pair symmetry of two-hole states using theory of invariants and the aid of numerical computations. Then, we review the charge stripe phase and calculate some of its properties within the t​-​t′​-​t′′​-​Jz{t\text{-}t^{\prime}\text{-}t^{\prime\prime}\text{-}J_{z}} model. Subsequently, we study the model subject to long-range repulsive interactions; and finally, the quantum pair-pair correlations of the full model is investigated and discuss on the emergence of dd- and pp- wave superconductivity triggered by the repulsive interactions.

IV.1 Symmetries in a square lattice with two holes

Let us consider the presence of two holes on a square lattice of size M×MM\times M , in the absence of long-range electron interactions, and periodic boundary conditions. A state |𝒌;𝑹⟩\ket{\bm k;\bm R} is invariant under g∈Gg\in G, where GG is a symmetry group that leaves the Hamiltonian invariant, if it satisfies

D^g​|𝒌;𝑹⟩=λg​|𝒌;𝑹⟩,\displaystyle\hat{D}_{g}\ket{\bm k;\bm R}=\lambda_{g}\ket{\bm k;\bm R}, (12)

where D^g\hat{D}_{g} is the unitary representation of gg and has eigenvalues λg≠0\lambda_{g}\neq 0. Then |𝒌;𝑹⟩\ket{\bm k;\bm R} is also eigenstate of every g′∈⟨g⟩g^{\prime}\in\langle g\rangle, the cyclic subgroup generated by gg. We call such states high-symmetry states. For a lattice point group and a state with zero total momentum, |𝒌=𝟎;𝑹⟩\ket{\bm k=\bm 0;\bm R}; the value of λg\lambda_{g} can only be ±1\pm 1. More precisely, λg=(−1)pg\lambda_{g}=(-1)^{p_{g}}, where pgp_{g} is the number of electron transpositions (electron pair exchanged) allowed by the symmetry operation gg. The point symmetry of the square lattice corresponds to the D4D_{4} point group, generated by a 90∘90^{\circ} clockwise rotation rr and a reflection ss about the bottom-left to top-right diagonal. The group has a total of five conjugacy classes, represented by the subsets {e}\{e\}, {r,r3}\{r,r^{3}\}, {r2}\{r^{2}\}, {s,s​r2}\{s,sr^{2}\}, and {s​r,s​r3}\{sr,sr^{3}\}, (see Table I).

For a M×MM\times M lattice containing two holes, the hole configuration may be invariant under a proper subgroup ℋ⊂D4{\cal H}\subset D_{4} of the full spatial point group, depending on the positions of the holes and if MM is even or odd. Three illustrative examples of such symmetries for the case of M≥4M\geq 4 with MM even are:

(a) Invariance under reflections about the horizontal and vertical axes (denoted, for example, by s​r3sr^{3} and s​rsr, respectively, if ss is the diagonal reflection), and under a 180∘180^{\circ} rotation r2r^{2}: (x,y)→(−x,−y)(x,y)\to(-x,-y) (Fig. 1(a)). The 180∘180^{\circ} rotation leaves four electrons invariant at the coordinate indices (0,0),(M/2,0),(0,M/2),(M/2,M/2)(0,0),(M/2,0),(0,M/2),(M/2,M/2). With two holes in the system (which are not exchanged under this operation), the number of exchanged electron pairs is (see Appendix A)

pr2=(M2−6)2,p_{r^{2}}=\frac{(M^{2}-6)}{2},

leading to λr2=−1\lambda_{r^{2}}=-1 for M≥4M\geq 4. This implies that λr3=−λr,λs=−λs​r2\lambda_{r^{3}}=-\lambda_{r},\lambda_{s}=-\lambda_{sr^{2}} and λs​r=−λs​r3\lambda_{sr}=-\lambda_{sr^{3}}. Entailing that the operations in two-elements equivalence classes have opposite sign.

Under the vertical reflection (x,y)→(−x,y)(x,y)\to(-x,y), and for even MM, the operation leaves two columns invariant: x=0x=0 and x=M/2x=M/2 (owing to the periodic boundary condition −x≡M−x(modM)-x\equiv M-x\pmod{M}. Assuming the two holes are placed in these fixed columns, they are not exchanged. The remaining M−2M-2 columns form (M−2)/2(M-2)/2 exchanged column pairs. Since each column contains MM sites, the total number of exchanged electron pairs is (see Appendix A)

ps​r3=M×M−22=M2​(M−2).p_{sr^{3}}=M\times\frac{M-2}{2}=\frac{M}{2}(M-2).

This number is always even for even M≥4M\geq 4, hence the eigenvalue of the reflection operator is λs​r3=(−1)ps​r3=1\lambda_{sr^{3}}=(-1)^{p_{sr^{3}}}=1.

(b) Invariance under reflection about the vertical axis (s​rsr); here the number of exchanged pairs is again ps​r=M⁡(M−2)/2p_{sr}=M(M-2)/2, giving λs​r=1\lambda_{sr}=1, note that in this case the first column 0 and M/2M/2 are invariant, (Fig.  1(b)).

(c) Invariance under reflection about the bottom-left to top-right diagonal (ss). In this special case, only the sites lying on the diagonal are invariant; the two holes are pinned to their sites and therefore are not exchanged This yields ps=(M2−M−2)/2p_{s}=(M^{2}-M-2)/2 exchanged electron pairs. The corresponding eigenvalue λs\lambda_{s} takes the value −1-1 when M/2M/2 is even, and +1+1 when M/2M/2 is odd, (Fig. 1(c)). Clearly the case λs=−1\lambda_{s}=-1 implies λs​r=−λr,λs​r2=−λr2,\lambda_{sr}=-\lambda_{r},\lambda_{sr^{2}}=-\lambda_{r^{2}}, and λs​r3=−λr3\lambda_{sr^{3}}=-\lambda_{r^{3}}.

To determine the symmetry of the ground state, we note that the Hamiltonian HH (Eq. 1) defined in a square lattice can be block-diagonalized into subspaces corresponding to the irrep of the spatial (non-magnetic) D4D_{4} symmetry group. The projection onto a given irrep Γ\Gamma is obtained using the projection operator,

P^Γ=dΓ|G|​∑gχgΓ​D^g,\displaystyle\hat{P}_{\Gamma}=\frac{d_{\Gamma}}{|G|}\sum_{g}\chi_{g}^{\Gamma}\hat{D}_{g}, (13)

where dΓd_{\Gamma} is the dimension of the irrep, |G||G| is the order of the group, χgΓ\chi^{\Gamma}_{g} is the character of gg for the irrep Γ\Gamma, and D^g\hat{D}_{g} is the representation of gg. The character table for the D4D_{4} symmetry group is shown in Table 1.

IV.2 Results for the tt-JzJ_{z} model with two holes

Using the numerical methodology described in Sec. III, we calculate the ground state of the tt-JzJ_{z} model (with t′=t′′=0t^{\prime}=t^{\prime\prime}=0, 𝒌=0\bm{k}=0, and Jz=0.4J_{z}=0.4) on an M×MM\times M two-dimensional lattice. We find that the ground state is two-fold degenerate for M=4,6,8,10,12M=4,6,8,10,12. The configuration shown in Fig. 1(a), which we denote as |ϕ(a)⟩|\phi_{\scriptscriptstyle{(a)}}\rangle, has a non-zero amplitude. Indeed, it is the most probable configuration for one of the two degenerate ground states.Note that the case M=6M=6 has been already studied by [40], though they do not discuss on the symmetries of the ground state.

The state |ϕ(a)⟩|\phi_{\scriptscriptstyle{(a)}}\rangle is characterized by the fact that P^Γ​|ϕ(a)⟩=0\hat{P}_{\Gamma}|\phi_{\scriptscriptstyle{(a)}}\rangle=0 for every irreducible representation Γ\Gamma except for Γ=χ5\Gamma=\chi_{5}. Since at least one of the two degenerate ground states has a non-zero projection onto |ϕ(a)⟩|\phi_{\scriptscriptstyle{(a)}}\rangle, we conclude that the ground state belongs to the χ5\chi_{5} (i.e., pp-wave) representation. Furthermore, the horizontal reflection preserves this state, while the vertical reflection changes its sign: D^s​r​|ϕ(a)⟩=|ϕ(a)⟩\hat{D}_{sr}|\phi_{\scriptscriptstyle{(a)}}\rangle=|\phi_{\scriptscriptstyle{(a)}}\rangle and D^s​r3​|ϕ(a)⟩=−|ϕ(a)⟩\hat{D}_{sr^{3}}|\phi_{\scriptscriptstyle{(a)}}\rangle=-|\phi_{\scriptscriptstyle{(a)}}\rangle. This identifies |ϕ(a)⟩|\phi_{\scriptscriptstyle{(a)}}\rangle as having pyp_{y}-like character, with its 90∘90^{\circ}-rotated partner exhibiting pxp_{x}-like character. Hence, from the numerical solution of the full degenerate ground state we can construct two orthogonal eigenstates: one with zero projection onto |ϕ(a)⟩|\phi_{\scriptscriptstyle{(a)}}\rangle -the domain of Fig.1(a)-, denoted |px⟩\ket{p_x}, and a second one corresponding to its orthogonal partner, denoted |py⟩\ket{p_y}.

On the other hand, we find that the first excited state is non-degenerate and therefore transforms according to a one-dimensional irreducible representation. Numerically, this state exhibits non-zero amplitudes for the configurations shown in Figs. 1(b) and 1(c), both are invariant under specific symmetry operations of D4D_{4}, which determines the irrep to which this state belongs.

For a one-dimensional irrep a symmetry operation D^g\hat{D}_{g} acts on a state |Ψ⟩|\Psi\rangle belonging to the irrep Γ\Gamma simply by the multiplication with the character χgΓ\chi_{g}^{\Gamma} [52]:

D^g​|Ψ⟩=χgΓ​|Ψ⟩.\displaystyle\hat{D}_{g}\ket{\Psi}=\chi_{g}^{\Gamma}\ket{\Psi}. (14)

Now consider the configuration Fig.1(b), embedded on a M×MM\times M the antiferromagnetic background with MM even ≥4\geq 4. Denoting this configuration as state |ϕ(b)⟩|\phi_{\scriptscriptstyle{(b)}}\rangle, and the first excited state as |Ψ⟩\ket{\Psi}, the matrix element of the reflection operator D^s​r\hat{D}_{sr} is given by

⟨ϕ(b)|​D^s​r​|Ψ⟩=χs​rΓ​⟨ϕ(b)|Ψ⟩.\displaystyle\bra{\phi_{(b)}}\hat{D}_{sr}\ket{\Psi}=\chi_{sr}^{\Gamma}\innerproduct{\phi_{(b)}}{\Psi}. (15)

If |ϕ(b)⟩\ket{\phi_{(b)}} is an eigenstate of D^s​r\hat{D}_{sr} with eigenvalue λs​r\lambda_{sr}, i.e., D^s​r​|ϕ(b)⟩=λs​r​|ϕ(b)⟩\hat{D}_{sr}\ket{\phi_{(b)}}=\lambda_{sr}\ket{\phi_{(b)}}, then a non-zero projection ⟨ϕ(b)|Ψ⟩\innerproduct{\phi_{(b)}}{\Psi} requires λs​r=χs​rΓ\lambda_{sr}=\chi_{sr}^{\Gamma}. Consequently, the only one-dimensional irreps allowing a non-zero amplitude for |ϕ(b)⟩\ket{\phi_{(b)}} are precisely those satisfying this condition, namely χ1\chi_{1} and χ4\chi_{4}.

Similarly, consider configuration (c) of Fig.1 embedded in the same M×MM\times M antiferromagnetic lattice. Denoting this configuration state as |ϕ(c)⟩\ket{\phi_{(c)}}, and the first excited state as |Ψ⟩\ket{\Psi}, the matrix element of the diagonal reflection D^s\hat{D}_{s} is given by

⟨ϕ(c)|​D^s​|Ψ⟩=χsΓ​⟨ϕ(c)|Ψ⟩.\displaystyle\bra{\phi_{(c)}}\hat{D}_{s}\ket{\Psi}=\chi_{s}^{\Gamma}\innerproduct{\phi_{(c)}}{\Psi}. (16)

If |ϕ(c)⟩\ket{\phi_{(c)}} is an eigenstate of D^s\hat{D}_{s} with eigenvalue λs\lambda_{s}, i.e., D^s​|ϕ(c)⟩=λs​|ϕ(c)⟩\hat{D}_{s}\ket{\phi_{(c)}}=\lambda_{s}\ket{\phi_{(c)}}, then a non-zero projection ⟨ϕ(c)|Ψ⟩\innerproduct{\phi_{(c)}}{\Psi} requires λs=χsΓ\lambda_{s}=\chi_{s}^{\Gamma}. As established earlier, λs=−1\lambda_{s}=-1 when M/2M/2 is even, and λs=+1\lambda_{s}=+1 when M/2M/2 is odd. Consequently, the state belongs to the χ4\chi_{4} irrep for M/2M/2 even (yielding dx2−y2d_{x^{2}-y^{2}} symmetry) and to the χ1\chi_{1} irrep for M/2M/2 odd (yielding ss-wave symmetry). We reserve the notation |dx2−y2⟩\ket{d_{x^2-y^2}} specifically for the even-M/2M/2 case.

In Fig.2 we show the numerical computations of the hole-hole correlation function Ch​(𝒓)=N⁡⟨h^𝒓​h^𝟎⟩C_{h}({\bm{r}})=N\langle\hat{h}_{\bm{r}}\hat{h}_{\bm{0}}\rangle of the tt-JzJ_{z} model (t=1t=1 and Jz=0.4J_{z}=0.4) in a 8×88\times 8 lattice with two holes for the ground (|px⟩\ket{p_x}) and first excited state (|dx2−y2⟩\ket{d_{x^2-y^2}}). Here h^𝒓\hat{h}_{\bm{r}} is the hole number operator at site 𝒓{\bm{r}} and NN is the total number of lattice sites. Note that the pp-wave state yields a dipolar correlation pattern, while a dx2−y2d_{x^{2}-y^{2}} state yields a quadrupolar one. The observed symmetry of Ch​(𝒓)C_{h}({\bm{r}}) is not a numerical artifact but a direct consequence of the transformation properties of the state. Since the density operator is a scalar under the point group, the correlation function inherits the same irreducible representation as the state from which it is computed.

IV.3 Effect of t′t^{\prime} and t′′t^{\prime\prime} in the tt-JzJ_{z} model

We now explore the effect of t′t^{\prime} and t′′t^{\prime\prime} on the ground-state symmetry and on hole-pair mobility, and subsequently examine the corresponding pairing-symmetry phase diagram. When finite values of t′t^{\prime} and t′′t^{\prime\prime} are included, additional hopping channels become available to the holes. Depending on the pair symmetry, these hoppings modify the energies and wavefunctions of the states, rendering them energetically more or less favorable.

In Fig. 4 we show the hole-hole correlation function Ch​(𝒓)C_{h}(\bm{r}) for,  4(a) the paired |px⟩\ket{p_x} state with t′=−0.3t^{\prime}=-0.3 and t′′=0.2t^{\prime\prime}=0.2 and for |dx2−y2⟩\ket{d_{x^2-y^2}} state with t′=0.3t^{\prime}=0.3 and t′′=−0.2t^{\prime\prime}=-0.2 ( 4(b)). The rest fo the parameters are as in Fig. 2. Compared with Fig. 2(b), the |dx2−y2⟩\ket{d_{x^2-y^2}} state is significantly modified by the additional hopping, resulting in a less localized pair. In contrast, the |px⟩\ket{p_x} state remains virtually unchanged by t′t^{\prime} and t′′t^{\prime\prime}.

To gain physical insight into the effect of t′t^{\prime} and t′′t^{\prime\prime}, we consider the possible hopping processes that allow a hole pair to propagate, as illustrated schematically in Fig. 3. The hopping tt mediates transitions to an excited virtual state, while t′t^{\prime} and t′′t^{\prime\prime} provide alternative connections between intermediate configurations. Specifically, the |px⟩\ket{p_x} state can propagate by (1,0)(1,0) through the intermediate virtual configuration (b1) via two tt-hopping steps. Note that (b1) is only accessible to |px⟩\ket{p_x}, while its projection onto (c2) vanishes. This corresponds to the sequence (a​1)→𝑡(b​1)→𝑡(c​1).(a1)\xrightarrow{\scriptscriptstyle{t}}(b1)\xrightarrow{\scriptscriptstyle{t}}(c1). However, the same final state (c1) can also be reached directly via a single t′′t^{\prime\prime} hopping.

These two possible paths to (c1) form a three-site loop, which can lead to geometric frustration. The product of the hopping amplitudes around this loop is t2​t′′.t^{2}t^{\prime\prime}. If this product is negative (i.e., t′′<0t^{\prime\prime}<0 for t>0t>0), the energy of a wavefunction occupying this loop is increased. Consequently, we expect a negative t′′t^{\prime\prime} to inhibit pp-wave pairing. This view will be supported by our numerical characterization of the hole-pairing symmetries shown below.

In a similar manner, the most probable configuration for |dx2−y2⟩\ket{d_{x^2-y^2}} is (b2). This state can propagate by (1/2,1/2)(1/2,1/2) via two alternative paths: either through two tt-hopping steps, (a​1)→𝑡(b​2)→𝑡(c​2),(a1)\xrightarrow{\scriptscriptstyle{t}}(b2)\xrightarrow{\scriptscriptstyle{t}}(c2), or directly through a single t′t^{\prime} hopping, (a​1)→t′(c​2).(a1)\xrightarrow{\scriptscriptstyle{t^{\prime}}}(c2). These two paths form a three-site loop with hopping product t2​t′t^{2}t^{\prime}. Since t>0t>0, a negative t′t^{\prime} makes this product negative, which increases the energy of a wavefunction occupying the loop—i.e., induces geometric frustration. Therefore, we expect t′<0t^{\prime}<0 to inhibit dx2−y2d_{x^{2}-y^{2}}-wave pairing, as predicted by our numerical analysis of the hole-pairing symmetries.

For the characterization of the hole-pairing symmetry, we identify the symmetry of the system’s states that yield a finite negative pairing energy, and we examine the absence of hole-position correlations. This is done as follows. Let us denote by ℰo\mathcal{E}_{o} the ground-state energy per hole of the interacting two-hole state—for instance, ℰp\mathcal{E}_{p} for the |px⟩\ket{p_x}-like state and ℰd\mathcal{E}_{d} for the |dx2−y2⟩\ket{d_{x^2-y^2}}-like state—and by ℰ2​h\mathcal{E}_{2h} the energy per hole of a completely unpaired reference state, |2​h⟩\ket{2h}, in which the two holes do not interact. Since the holes are noninteracting in this reference state, its energy per hole is approximately twice the single-hole energy, ℰ2​h≈2​ℰ1​h{\cal E}_{2h}\approx 2{\cal E}_{1h}, where ℰ1​h{\cal E}_{1h} is the ground-state energy of the Hamiltonian with a single hole. The binding energy per hole is the defined as ℰb=ℰo−ℰ2​h.{\cal E}_{b}={\cal E}_{o}-{\cal E}_{2h}. A negative value of ℰb{\cal E}_{b} indicates that pairing is energetically favorable relative to the unpaired reference state. We confirm that |2​h⟩\ket{2h} is an unpaired state by examining its spatial density correlations; the hole-hole correlation function remains essentially constant across all site separations, ⟨h^𝒓​h^𝟎⟩≈const\langle\hat{h}_{\bm{r}}\hat{h}_{\bm{0}}\rangle\approx\text{const}. Consequently, hole pairing is energetically favorable (and thermodynamically stable) whenever ℰb<0{\cal E}_{b}<0.

In Fig. 5, we present the pairing phase diagram as a function of t′t^{\prime} and t′′t^{\prime\prime} obtained from our numerical calculations for a 8×88\times 8 lattice with two holes and J=0.4,t=1J=0.4,t=1 and V=0V=0. Black regions describes regimes where hole pairing is energetically unfavorable, meaning ℰb≥0{\cal E}_{b}\geq 0 across all configurations. Conversely, red (blue) colors mark the parameter space where the |px⟩\ket{p_x} (|dx2−y2⟩\ket{d_{x^2-y^2}}) state forms a stable bound pair with a negative binding energy (ℰb<0{\cal E}_{b}<0). The pink region highlights the regime where both the pp-wave and dd-wave pairs are simultaneously favorable relative to the unpaired |2​h⟩\ket{2h} state. These numerical results are in concordance with our preceding analysis. For instance, for parameters commonly associated with hole-doped cuprates (t′=−0.3t^{\prime}=-0.3, t′′=0.2t^{\prime\prime}=0.2)[63, 8], this model predicts a ground state characterized by pp-wave pairing symmetry and for electron-doped cuprates dd-wave symmetry (t′=0.3t^{\prime}=0.3, t′′=−0.2t^{\prime\prime}=-0.2)[63, 8].

IV.4 Stripe phase

As mentioned in the introduction, stripe phases can form in strongly correlated electron materials, most notably in the cuprate high-temperature superconductors. They correspond to a modulated electronic state characterized by coupled unidirectional patterns of charge and spin: charge-density waves (CDW) and spin-density waves (SDW). The wavelengths of these modulations obey the relation λSDW=2​λCDW\lambda_{\text{SDW}}=2\lambda_{\text{CDW}}.[13, 62] Such CDW/SDW order separates two distinct antiferromagnetic domains, effectively acting as an antiphase domain wall. In LSCO-based materials, this stripe order has been observed in the doping range ∼0.1<δ<0.135\sim\!0.1<\delta<0.135 and is strongest at the commensurate doping level δ∼1/8\delta\sim 1/8 [55].

In what follows, we analyze stripe phases arising within the tt-t′t^{\prime}-t′′t^{\prime\prime}-JzJ_{z} model for systems with a small even number of holes (global hole densities δ≲0.15\delta\lesssim 0.15) with parameters for a hole-doped cuprate J=0.4J=0.4, t=1t=1, t′=−0.3t^{\prime}=-0.3 and t′′=0.2t^{\prime\prime}=0.2. Specifically, we examine 5×M5\times M lattices, with MM even and M>5M>5, under periodic boundary conditions. Two sets of calculations are performed: (i) using 4 holes, which yields linear hole densities along the stripe ρl=4/M=0.4,0.5,2/3\rho_{l}=4/M=0.4,0.5,2/3 for M=10,8,6M=10,8,6, respectively; and (ii) using 2 holes, giving ρl=2/M=1/3,0.25,0.2\rho_{l}=2/M=1/3,0.25,0.2 for M=6,8,10M=6,8,10, respectively. Our calculations show that such geometry configuration and set of parameters yields the formation of a horizontal antiphase domain wall of length MM, characterized by a line of wrong bonds where neighboring sites along the vertical direction have the same spin orientation, i.e., Sz​(x,y)​Sz​(x,y+1)=1/4S^{z}(x,y)S^{z}(x,y+1)=1/4 for x∈{0,1,…,L−1}x\in\{0,1,\ldots,L-1\} for some 0≤y<M0\leq y<M, instead of the staggered spin configuration. As an example we show in Fig.6 the ground state spin configuration for a 5×65\times 6 lattice with two holes (δ=0.067\delta=0.067) thats shows a linear stripe with ρl=1/3\rho_{l}=1/3.

Regarding the energy cost of adding holes to a unidirectional stripe, Chernyshev et al. [14] analyzed this problem within the tt-JzJ_{z} model under the rigid band approximation. They found that the process is equivalent to adding holes to a strictly one-dimensional system, and the resulting energy is given by

ℰS=Jz2​ρl+A​cos⁡(π​ρl)+B,\displaystyle{\cal E}_{S}=\frac{J_{z}}{2\rho_{l}}+A\cos(\pi\rho_l)+B, (17)

where AA and BB are constants for fixed JzJ_{z} and tt. In this expression, the first term corresponds to the domain-wall energy, while the second term arises from the kinetic energy of free particles filling the one-dimensional band up to the Fermi wavevector kF=π​ρlk_{F}=\pi\rho_{l} [14].

We have calculated the energy per hole ℰS{\cal E}_{S} for a single stripe, as well as the one shifted respect to the domain wall energy, (ℰS−Jz/2​ρl{\cal E}_{S}-J_{z}/2\rho_{l}) as a function of hole filling ρl\rho_{l} in 5×M5\times M lattices (MM even). A comparison of our numerical calculations with the analytical results of Eq. (17) gives us a reasonable good agreement by fitting A=−0.296A=-0.296 and B=−2.652B=-2.652 (Fig. 7) It is notable the agreement despite the fact that including t′t^{\prime} and t′′t^{\prime\prime} hoppings goes beyond the rigid band approximation.

The optimal filling that minimizes ℰS\mathcal{E}_{S} for a stripe is ρlop≈0.5\rho_{l}^{\text{op}}\approx 0.5, consistent with other numerical results (Fig. 7(b)) [61, 11, 60]. A dashed horizontal line is drawn at the ground-state energy (per hole) of the interacting pair state in the dilute regime, ℰp=−2.16\mathcal{E}_{p}=-2.16. The energy difference (per hole) between the optimally filled stripe and the pair is therefore ℰS−ℰp≈−0.1\mathcal{E}_{S}-\mathcal{E}_{p}\approx-0.1.

The numerical results show that holes will tend to form the structures of lowest possible energy, and in large systems, in the absence for long-range interactions, they will try to form half-filled stripes with separation L≥5L\geq 5, whenever possible. Thus, the half-filled ρl=0.5\rho_{l}=0.5 striped phase is the ground state for δ=ρl/L≤0.1\delta=\rho_{l}/L\leq 0.1. Similarly, a stripe with 0.5≤ρl<0.750.5\leq\rho_{l}<0.75 has lower energy than hole pairs (or unpaired holes), so the ground state remains striped with ρl≥0.5\rho_{l}\geq 0.5 for doping 0.1≤δ≤0.150.1\leq\delta\leq 0.15.

IV.5 Long-range repulsive interaction

We now extend the tt-t′t^{\prime}-t′′t^{\prime\prime}-JzJ_{z} model by including electron-electron interactions beyond the on-site Hubbard UU, namely long-range Coulomb or short-range Yukawa/dipolar potentials. Let us first analyze the exchange energy of a system containing two holes in the absence of such interactions, in a simplified but illustrative manner. For two holes at adjacent sites (r=1r=1), the number of broken antiferromagnetic bonds relative to the Néel state is seven, corresponding to a magnetic energy cost of 7​J/27J/2. For r>1r>1, the minimal magnetic cost is 8​J/28J/2. Thus, bringing the holes close together reduces the magnetic energy by J/2J/2. Adding a repulsive electric potential modifies this energy landscape. The total potential energy can be written then as the sum of the magnetic and electric contributions, Epot=EM+EVE_{\text{pot}}=E_{M}+E_{V}, where EM=⟨Ψ|​HJz​|Ψ⟩E_{M}=\bra{\Psi}H_{J_{z}}\ket{\Psi}, and

EV=V2​⟨Ψ|​∑𝒋≠𝒊f⁡(|𝒊−𝒋|)​n^𝒊​n^𝒋​|Ψ⟩,\displaystyle E_{V}=\frac{V}{2}\bra{\Psi}\sum_{\bm{j}\neq\bm{i}}f(|\bm{i}-\bm{j}|)\,\hat{n}_{\bm{i}}\hat{n}_{\bm{j}}\ket{\Psi}, (18)

with f⁡(r)f(r) a function of the hole separation r=|𝒊−𝒋|r=|\bm{i}-\bm{j}|.

We consider several functional forms for the repulsive potential: f⁡(r)=0f(r)=0 (no repulsion), f⁡(r)=1/rf(r)=1/r (long-range Coulomb), f⁡(r)=e−r/rf(r)=e^{-r}/r (Yukawa, corresponding to Thomas–Fermi screening), and f⁡(r)=1/r3f(r)=1/r^{3} (dipolar-like interaction). For f⁡(r)=0f(r)=0, the total potential energy Epot​(r)E_{\text{pot}}(r) exhibits a characteristic pocket with a minimum at r=1r=1, giving rise to an effective attractive force between the holes (Fig.8). This attraction can be strong enough to drive phase separation. Introducing a short-range repulsive potential (such as Yukawa or dipolar) tends to fill or eliminate this pocket, depending on the value of VV, thereby suppressing pairing. By contrast, the long-range Coulomb repulsion, which decays more slowly, appears to be the most suitable candidate for modifying the energy landscape while preserving a viable pairing mechanism.

We have found that for two holes in a 6×66\times 6 lattice (δ=0.055\delta=0.055) with J=0.4,t=1,t′=−0.3,t′′=0.2J=0.4,t=1,t^{\prime}=-0.3,t^{\prime\prime}=0.2, the ground state is paired up to V=2.7V=2.7. This result is close to the estimate by Calzado et al.[28]. For two holes in an 8×88\times 8 lattice (δ=0.031\delta=0.031), the ground state is paired up to V≈1V\approx 1. Given that it is known that superconductivity appears in LSCO materials at δ=0.055\delta=0.055, we consider V≈3V\approx 3 to be a realistic value, with V=1V=1 as a lower bound.

For the stripe geometry, specifically on an 11×411\times 4 lattice with line density ρl=0.5\rho_{l}=0.5, we find that the long-range Coulomb interaction expels a hole from the stripe already at V≈1.8V\approx 1.8 (see Fig. 9). In contrast, short-range interactions, such as 1/r31/r^{3} and Yukawa potentials, require a higher coupling, V≈2.3V\approx 2.3, to induce hole expulsion. For purely next-nearest-neighbor repulsion, the threshold increases even further to V>6V>6. Thus, long-range interactions destabilize the half-filled stripe, whereas shorter-range interactions tend to stabilize it. Moreover, since next-nearest-neighbor repulsion alone cannot expel a hole for ρl≤0.5\rho_{l}\leq 0.5 at realistic values of VV—and short-range repulsions generally have a weaker effect at lower densities—the stripe phase is expected to dominate at low doping (δ<0.10\delta<0.10) in the extended Hubbard model.

IV.6 Pair expulsion from the stripe

Let us consider two characteristic ground states. One is the pure stripe state, which is the ground state near half-filling at V=0V=0, and denoted by |S⟩\ket{S} with energy per hole ℰS\mathcal{E}_{S} . The other, denoted |S+p⟩\ket{S+p}, consists of a stripe plus an expelled hole pair oriented parallel to it with ground state ℰS+p\mathcal{E}_{S+p} (See Fig.10). Using these two states as trial wavefunctions, we apply then the Lanczos-based algorithm [54] for increasing values of the truncation parameter nn, up to n∼107n\sim 10^{7}. We consider lattice sizes 12×712\times 7, 12×512\times 5, 10×510\times 5, and 8×58\times 5, each containing six holes, which correspond to dopings δ=0.07,0.10,0.12,\delta=0.07,0.10,0.12, and 0.150.15, respectively.

We find that the energy of a trial state follows a power law in the number of retained states,

ℰ⁡(n)=ℰ∞+b​nC,\mathcal{E}(n)=\mathcal{E}^{\infty}+bn^{C},

where ℰ∞\mathcal{E}^{\infty} is the true ground-state energy, and bb and CC are constants. Consequently, the energy difference between the two competing states as a function of nn is

ℰS+p​(n)−ℰS​(n)=ℰS+p∞−ℰS∞+b1​nC1−b2​nC2.\mathcal{E}_{S+p}(n)-\mathcal{E}_{S}(n)=\mathcal{E}_{S+p}^{\infty}-\mathcal{E}_{S}^{\infty}+b_{1}n^{C_{1}}-b_{2}n^{C_{2}}.

For sufficiently large nn, the term with the largest exponent dominates. In Fig. 11, we show the evolution of the variational energy ℰt−Jz{\cal E}_{t-J_{z}} and the energy difference ℰS−ℰS+p\mathcal{E}_{S}-\mathcal{E}_{S+p} for the two competing states with six holes and parameters V=3V=3, J=0.4J=0.4, t=1t=1, t′=−0.3t^{\prime}=-0.3, and t′′=0.2t^{\prime\prime}=0.2. For δ=0.10\delta=0.10 (12×512\times 5 lattice, stripe filling ρl=0.5\rho_{l}=0.5), the pure stripe state has lower energy than the stripe-plus-pair state. In this case, the reduction in potential energy from expelling the pair is insufficient to overcome the energy cost of disrupting the stripe. Conversely, for δ=0.07\delta=0.07 (12×712\times 7 lattice, also with ρl=0.5\rho_{l}=0.5), the increased system width of 7 makes hole expulsion energetically favorable. At δ=0.12\delta=0.12 (10×510\times 5 lattice), the two states become nearly degenerate, whereas for δ=0.15\delta=0.15 (8×58\times 5 lattice), the stripe-plus-pair state is actually lower in energy than the pure stripe. For these latter two dopings, the stripe filling is higher than the optimal ρl=0.5\rho_{l}=0.5; expelling holes reduces the filling within the stripe, which stabilizes the remaining holes inside and allows the expelled pairs to exist outside the stripe.

This charge expulsion from the stripe, enabled by the long-range repulsive interaction, constitutes the key mechanism for superconductivity in this model over the doping range 0.05<δ<0.150.05<\delta<0.15, as we will show below through the pairing correlation calculations.

IV.7 Pairing correlations

We have already shown that the holes expelled from the stripe by the long-range repulsion form bound states (ℰb<0\mathcal{E}_{b}<0). The remaining question is whether these bound states coherently propagate and establish long-range phase coherence—i.e., whether they exhibit superconducting behavior.

To probe superconductivity in these states, we have numerically calculated the triplet pair–pair correlation function[56],

Px​x​(𝒓)=⟨Δx†​(𝒓)​Δx​(0)⟩,\displaystyle P_{xx}(\bm{r})=\langle\Delta_{x}^{\dagger}(\bm{r})\Delta_{x}(0)\rangle, (19)

where

Δx​(𝒓)=12​(c𝒓+e^x,↑​c𝒓,↓+c𝒓+e^x,↓​c𝒓,↑).\displaystyle\Delta_{x}(\bm{r})=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(c_{\bm{r}+\hat{e}_{x},\uparrow}c_{\bm{r},\downarrow}+c_{\bm{r}+\hat{e}_{x},\downarrow}c_{\bm{r},\uparrow}\right). (20)

The operator Δx†​(𝒓)\Delta_{x}^{\dagger}(\bm{r}) creates a spin-triplet Cooper pair on the nearest-neighbor bond along the xx-direction, centered at site 𝒓\bm{r}. The function Px​x​(𝒓)P_{xx}(\bm{r}) thus measures the spatial coherence of pairing, i.e., the correlation between the amplitude to create a pair at the origin and the amplitude to annihilate a pair at position 𝒓\bm{r}.

The pair–pair correlation function for a given distance |𝒓||\bm{r}| is then defined as

Px​x​(|𝒓|)=∑|𝒓′|=|𝒓|Px​x​(𝒓′)N|𝒓|,\displaystyle P_{xx}(|\bm{r}|)=\sum_{|\bm{r}^{\prime}|=|\bm{r}|}\frac{P_{xx}(\bm{r}^{\prime})}{N_{|\bm{r}|}}, (21)

where N|𝒓|N_{|\bm{r}|} is the number of lattice vectors with length |𝒓||\bm{r}|. In a superconducting state, Px​x​(|𝒓|)P_{xx}(|\bm{r}|) should decay at most as a power law as |𝒓|→∞|\bm{r}|\to\infty, whereas in a non-superconducting state—such as an insulator or a normal metal with local pairing—it decays exponentially [57, 58].

We plot Px​x​(|𝒓|)P_{xx}(|\bm{r}|) in Fig. 12 for the horizontally aligned pair |px⟩\ket{p_x}, the vertically aligned pair |py⟩\ket{p_y}, two unpaired holes |2​h⟩\ket{2h}, and the half-filled four-hole stripe |S⟩\ket{S}, all on an 8×58\times 5 lattice. As shown in the figure, Px​x​(|𝒓|)P_{xx}(|\bm{r}|) decays exponentially for all states except for the |px⟩\ket{p_x} pair, which exhibits off-diagonal long-range order (ODLRO)—a hallmark of superconductivity. We attribute this true ODLRO to the neglect of spin dynamics in the model. A similar analysis of Py​y​(|𝒓|)P_{yy}(|\bm{r}|) reveals that |py⟩\ket{p_y} also displays superconducting behavior. Interestingly, while stripes with ρl=1\rho_{l}=1 and ρl≤0.5\rho_{l}\leq 0.5 show no signs of superconductivity, we find that stripes with filling ρl=0.6¯\rho_{l}=0.\bar{6} do exhibit superconducting features.

In Fig. 13(a), we show Px​x​(|𝒓|)P_{xx}(|\bm{r}|) for three states: a horizontal stripe with filling ρl=0.6¯\rho_{l}=0.\bar{6} (|S⟩\ket{S}), a horizontal stripe plus a horizontally aligned pair (|S+px⟩\ket{S+p_x}), and a horizontal stripe with a vertically aligned pair (|S+py⟩\ket{S+p_y}). The correlation function for |S+px⟩\ket{S+p_x} indicates that pxp_{x} pairs can coexist on opposite sides of the system, as Px​x​(|𝒓|)P_{xx}(|\bm{r}|) does not vanish as |𝒓|→∞|\bm{r}|\to\infty. Remarkably, the pure stripe |S⟩\ket{S} with ρl=0.6¯\rho_{l}=0.\bar{6} also exhibits a non-zero asymptotic value of Px​x​(|𝒓|)P_{xx}(|\bm{r}|), suggesting that it exchanges pxp_{x} pairs with the surrounding medium—since the pairs and the stripe holes occupy opposite sides of the lattice. In fact, the superconducting properties of the pure stripe |S⟩\ket{S} are comparable to those of the stripe with a pxp_{x} pair, |S+px⟩\ket{S+p_x}. In contrast, the stripe with a vertically aligned pair, |S+py⟩\ket{S+p_y}, shows an exponentially decaying Px​x​(|𝒓|)P_{xx}(|\bm{r}|), indicating no pxp_{x}-pairing character.

Finally, in Fig. 13(b), we present the superconducting phase diagram as a function of doping δ\delta and repulsive interaction strength VV, for fixed parameters J=0.4J=0.4, t=1t=1, t′=−0.3t^{\prime}=-0.3, and t′′=0.2t^{\prime\prime}=0.2. The phase diagram is constructed by plotting the energy difference Δ​E=ℰS+p−ℰS\Delta E=\mathcal{E}_{S+p}-\mathcal{E}_{S} between the pure stripe state |S⟩\ket{S} and the stripe-plus-pair state |S+p⟩\ket{S+p}. A negative value of Δ​E\Delta E indicates that the stripe-plus-pair state (i.e., a superconducting-like phase) is energetically favored.

At V=0V=0, the pure stripe phase is dominant across all dopings. In contrast, for V=3V=3, we observe a reentrant behavior: the system is superconducting-like at δ≈0.07\delta\approx 0.07, becomes non-superconducting (half-filled stripe dominant) in the doping range 0.10≲δ≲0.120.10\lesssim\delta\lesssim 0.12, and re-enters the superconducting regime for δ>0.12\delta>0.12. This sequence of phases closely resembles the behavior observed in Nd-LSCO (neodymium-doped La2-xSrxCuO4) [59].

V Concluding Remarks

In this work, we have investigated the pairing symmetry and superconducting properties of an extended two-dimensional tt-t′t^{\prime}-t′′t^{\prime\prime}-JzJ_{z} model, treating anisotropic Ising-like magnetic interactions and long-range electron–electron repulsions within an unified framework. We show that depending upon the sign and magnitude of t′t^{\prime} and t′′t^{\prime\prime} hopping parameters a dominant pp-wave, dd-wave or coexistence of both symmetries may be present, underscoring the crucial role of t′t^{\prime} and t′′t^{\prime\prime} in determining the pairing channel. We further find that long-range repulsive interactions in the low doping regime (δ≈0.7\delta\approx 0.7) can expel hole pairs from these non-superconducting stripe domains, thereby stabilizing a superconducting phase.

The calculated superconducting phase diagram exhibits a behavior that closely resembles experimental observations in hole-doped cuprates, such as Nd-LSCO (neodymium-doped La2-xSrxCuO4) [59]. Moreover, our pairing correlation calculations strongly indicate that repulsive Coulomb interactions drive reentrant superconductivity at doping levels between δ≈0.07\delta\approx 0.07 and δ≈0.15\delta\approx 0.15, consistent with phenomena reported in niobium-based cuprates. We believe that these results highlight the essential role of long-range electrostatic repulsions in strongly correlated systems and provide a solid groundwork for further theoretical analyses of unconventional superconducting mechanisms.

Symmetry operations and pair counting

We consider an M×MM\times M square lattice (MM even, M≥4M\geq 4) with periodic boundary conditions. The point group D4D_{4} is generated by the diagonal reflection s:(x,y)→(y,x)s:(x,y)\to(y,x) and the 90∘ rotation r:(x,y)→(y,−x)r:(x,y)\to(y,-x). In the main text we use the operations

s:(x,y)\displaystyle s:(x,y) →(y,x)\displaystyle\to(y,x)
r2:(x,y)\displaystyle r^{2}:(x,y) →(−x,−y)\displaystyle\to(-x,-y)
s​r:(x,y)\displaystyle sr:(x,y) →(−x,y)\displaystyle\to(-x,y)

The staggered antiferromagnetic background is defined by Sz​(x,y)=(−1)x+y/2S^{z}(x,y)=(-1)^{x+y}/2, and is invariant under all three operations, since −x-x and −y-y have the same parity as xx and yy.

The three hole configurations of Fig. 1 are invariant under the following operations, yielding the corresponding numbers of exchanged electron pairs pp:

Configuration (a) |ϕ(a)⟩\ket{\phi_{(a)}}: holes at (0,1)(0,1) and (0,−1)(0,-1); Sz(0,0)=−1/2S^{z}(0,0)=-1/2. Invariant under r2r^{2}. pr2=M2−62.p_{r^{2}}=\frac{M^{2}-6}{2}.

Configuration (b) |ϕ(b)⟩\ket{\phi_{(b)}}: holes at (0,0)(0,0) and (0,1)(0,1). Invariant under s​rsr. Fixed columns: x=0x=0 and x=M/2x=M/2, containing 2​M2M sites; two holes lie on these columns, so invariant electrons are 2​M−22M-2. Exchanged electrons (M2−2)−(2​M−2)=M⁡(M−2)(M^{2}-2)-(2M-2)=M(M-2), hence

ps​r=M⁡(M−2)2.p_{sr}=\frac{M(M-2)}{2}.

Configuration (c) |ϕ(c)⟩\ket{\phi_{(c)}}: holes at (1,0)(1,0) and (0,1)(0,1); Sz(0,0)=−1/2S^{z}(0,0)=-1/2. Invariant under ss. Fixed diagonal: MM sites. Off-diagonal electrons (M2−M)−2=M2−M−2(M^{2}-M)-2=M^{2}-M-2, hence
